Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings: Acute onset dysuria with malodorous urine, suprapubic pain, and microscopic/macroscopic hematuria in an otherwise healthy 50-year-old woman; no systemic or upper-tract features.

Working diagnosis: Acute uncomplicated bacterial cystitis – most likely (high likelihood per DDx and clinical presentation).

Differential diagnoses (consistent with transcript):
• Urethritis due to STI (Chlamydia/Gonorrhoea) – moderate likelihood; limited sexual history, no discharge.  
• Distal ureteric or bladder calculus – low–moderate likelihood; hematuria present but no colicky flank pain.

Management priorities: Prompt empiric oral antibiotics for 3 days; hydration advice; urinary alkalinizing sachets; consider urine dip/culture and STI screen if symptoms persist or recur; safety-netting for escalation (fever, flank pain, retention, recurrent episodes).

Management Plan

- Prescription: 3-day course of oral antibiotics (specific agent not documented).  
- Dispensing: Sent electronically to patient’s nominated pharmacy (Knightsbridge Practice); advised collection within ~1 hour.  
- Self-care advice: Increase fluid intake to 2.5–3 L/day; optional cranberry juice; OTC urinary alkalinizing sachets (details to be provided in notes).  
- Monitoring: Obtain home thermometer to check temperature; advised to seek review if fever, worsening pain, back/loin pain, urinary retention, or lack of improvement.  
- Follow-up: No routine follow-up if symptoms resolve; re-consult if recurrent or persistent.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Acute uncomplicated bacterial cystitis – High likelihood: classic dysuria, foul urine odor, suprapubic pain, hematuria; no systemic signs.  
2. Urethritis (Chlamydia/Gonorrhoea) – Moderate likelihood: dysuria ± hematuria without fever; sexual risk not fully assessed.  
3. Urinary tract calculi – Low–Moderate likelihood: hematuria and pain possible, but absence of flank pain and colic.
